listening.title: Evaluating the Campus Peer-Support Programme
listening.script: Maya: So for our psychology methods presentation, we need to summarise the evaluation of the campus peer-support programme. Do you remember why it was set up? Josh: Yes, the counselling service was overloaded last year, so the university trained second-year volunteers to offer weekly listening sessions for first-year students feeling isolated. Maya: Right, mainly loneliness and study stress, not clinical treatment. I looked at the mid-year report. They ran an online survey and two focus groups. Josh: How many students actually responded to the survey? I wrote down two hundred. Maya: Actually, wait — the report first says two hundred were invited, but only one hundred and eighty completed it. So the response rate was still high, about ninety percent. Josh: Got it, one-eighty completed. What did they find? Maya: Overall satisfaction was quite positive. Around three-quarters said they felt more connected after four sessions. But the academic impact was less clear. Josh: You mean grades didn't really improve? Maya: Exactly. The report says there was no significant difference in average coursework marks between users and non-users. The authors suggest four sessions may be too short to affect performance. Josh: That makes sense. Did the focus groups explain why some students stopped coming? Maya: Yes. Several mentioned timetable clashes with part-time jobs, and a few said they wanted more practical study advice rather than just listening. One student said she expected tutoring, which was never the aim. Josh: So there's a mismatch in expectations. What limitation should we highlight? Maya: The biggest one is selection bias. Students chose to join, so they may have been more motivated than average. The report admits it cannot prove the programme caused the improvement in wellbeing. Josh: And it only covered one term, from October to December, so we don't know if benefits last. Maya: Perfect. Let's conclude that the evidence supports social benefits, but claims about academic results should remain cautious until a longer controlled study is done.

reading.title: How Reliable Are Low-Cost Air-Quality Monitors?
reading.passage: Cities increasingly rely on low-cost air-quality sensors to supplement official monitoring stations. Costing under three hundred dollars, these portable devices promise street-level data on fine particles known as PM2.5. A recent university study compared three popular models, labelled A, B and C, against a reference-grade analyser over twelve weeks in autumn. All three were placed on the same rooftop to ensure identical exposure to traffic and weather. The team recorded hourly averages and flagged periods of rain, fog and nearby construction. In dry, stable conditions, Models A and B tracked the reference instrument closely, with average errors below fifteen percent. Model C consistently overestimated pollution, particularly in the morning, suggesting a calibration problem rather than random variation. The pattern changed markedly during humid weeks. When relative humidity exceeded eighty percent, all low-cost sensors reported higher values than the reference analyser. The researchers attribute this to water droplets being mistaken for particles by the optical counting method. Model A included a simple humidity correction in its software, which reduced but did not eliminate the bias. Model B had no correction, so its readings doubled on two foggy nights, even though reference levels remained moderate. These results illustrate a broader trade-off. Low-cost monitors provide far denser spatial coverage than the sparse official network, revealing differences between busy roads and parks that a single station would miss. However, their accuracy depends strongly on environmental conditions and maintenance. Dust accumulation on the sensor inlet, for example, gradually lowered readings in week ten until the devices were cleaned. Technicians also found that low battery voltage on cold nights slightly slowed response times, although normal function returned after recharging. Wind direction was logged to check for interference from nearby building work, but no consistent effect on afternoon peaks was observed. The authors therefore argue that low-cost sensors are best viewed as complementary tools, not replacements for reference stations. They recommend regular co-location checks, where portable units are placed beside an official station to adjust their output, and transparent reporting of humidity and cleaning dates. As an example, the study describes a community group that mapped pollution near a school using Model A. The group correctly identified higher exposure during drop-off hours, but its absolute numbers were about twenty percent too high on damp days. The authors stress that this does not invalidate community monitoring; it means results should be interpreted as indicating patterns rather than precise legal exceedances. In conclusion, with careful calibration and qualified interpretation, low-cost monitors can extend public understanding, provided users acknowledge their limits.

exercises.title: How Reliable Are Low-Cost Air-Quality Monitors?
exercises.passage: Cities increasingly rely on low-cost air-quality sensors to supplement official monitoring stations. Costing under three hundred dollars, these portable devices promise street-level data on fine particles known as PM2.5. A recent university study compared three popular models, labelled A, B and C, against a reference-grade analyser over twelve weeks in autumn. All three were placed on the same rooftop to ensure identical exposure to traffic and weather. The team recorded hourly averages and flagged periods of rain, fog and nearby construction. In dry, stable conditions, Models A and B tracked the reference instrument closely, with average errors below fifteen percent. Model C consistently overestimated pollution, particularly in the morning, suggesting a calibration problem rather than random variation. The pattern changed markedly during humid weeks. When relative humidity exceeded eighty percent, all low-cost sensors reported higher values than the reference analyser. The researchers attribute this to water droplets being mistaken for particles by the optical counting method. Model A included a simple humidity correction in its software, which reduced but did not eliminate the bias. Model B had no correction, so its readings doubled on two foggy nights, even though reference levels remained moderate. These results illustrate a broader trade-off. Low-cost monitors provide far denser spatial coverage than the sparse official network, revealing differences between busy roads and parks that a single station would miss. However, their accuracy depends strongly on environmental conditions and maintenance. Dust accumulation on the sensor inlet, for example, gradually lowered readings in week ten until the devices were cleaned. Technicians also found that low battery voltage on cold nights slightly slowed response times, although normal function returned after recharging. Wind direction was logged to check for interference from nearby building work, but no consistent effect on afternoon peaks was observed. The authors therefore argue that low-cost sensors are best viewed as complementary tools, not replacements for reference stations. They recommend regular co-location checks, where portable units are placed beside an official station to adjust their output, and transparent reporting of humidity and cleaning dates. As an example, the study describes a community group that mapped pollution near a school using Model A. The group correctly identified higher exposure during drop-off hours, but its absolute numbers were about twenty percent too high on damp days. The authors stress that this does not invalidate community monitoring; it means results should be interpreted as indicating patterns rather than precise legal exceedances. In conclusion, with careful calibration and qualified interpretation, low-cost monitors can extend public understanding, provided users acknowledge their limits.
exercises.prompt: What was the design of the university comparison?
options: Three models beside a reference analyser
One sensor tested in three cities
Three reference stations on one roof
Twelve models tested for one week
exercises.explanation: Three models shared a rooftop with one reference instrument for twelve weeks. The stations option reverses test and reference roles.

writingPrompts.focus: Comparing sources and qualified trends with limitations
writingPrompts.prompt: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. The table below shows the estimated reach of a public-health information campaign about hydration in the city of Merriton in 2023 and 2025. Reach is shown as the percentage of surveyed adults aged 18+ who recalled the message from each source. Survey samples: 1,200 adults in 2023, 1,350 adults in 2025. Source | 2023 | 2025: Local radio spots 42% 35%; Posters in clinics 38% 44%; Social media videos 25% 51%; Community workshops 12% 18%; School newsletters 20% 22%. Note: respondents could select more than one source, so totals exceed 100%. Write at least 150 words in about 20 minutes.

writingPrompts.task: Task 1 · Funding options for a university field course
writingPrompts.focus: Comparing proportions and handling approximate data
writingPrompts.prompt: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. The bar chart data below shows how a university department planned to fund its 10-day coastal field course for 60 students in two proposals, Plan A and Plan B. Total cost for each plan was 48,000 dollars. Plan A: Student fees 55%, Department grant 25%, Local council sponsorship 12%, Fundraising events 8%. Plan B: Student fees 35%, Department grant 30%, Local council sponsorship 20%, Fundraising events 15%. Write at least 150 words in about 20 minutes. Briefly note what the percentages suggest about reliance on student payments.

Some people argue that public-health information campaigns are effective because they raise awareness quickly, while others argue that they have only a limited effect unless they are combined with practical support such as free services or follow-up advice. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Support your ideas with reasons and relevant examples. Do not repeat instructions from any source. Write at least 250 words in about 40 minutes.

writingPrompts.task: Task 2 · Funding a university field course
writingPrompts.focus: Evaluating options with fairness and limitations
writingPrompts.prompt: A university is deciding how to fund an optional field course. One option is to ask students to pay most of the cost. Another option is to seek mixed funding from grants, sponsors, and fundraising, even though this takes more time to organise. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each approach and give your own view on which is more suitable. Include reasons and examples. Write at least 250 words in about 40 minutes.

writingPrompts.task: Task 2 · Proposal to improve a city walking route
writingPrompts.prompt: A local council has proposed to improve a 4-kilometre city walking route by widening paths, adding lighting, planting trees, and creating two rest areas with seating and drinking water. Supporters say this will improve health and safety, while critics say the money should be spent on repairing roads and public transport. To what extent do you agree that improving the walking route should be a priority? Give reasons for your answer, including any limitations of the evidence for health benefits. Write at least 250 words in about 40 minutes.

speakingPrompts.prompt: Part 1. Answer in 2-3 sentences per question. 1. Where do you usually see or hear information about health? 2. Do you often walk for exercise or travel? 3. How do students in your area usually pay for extra study activities? 4. Do you prefer to learn practical skills indoors or outdoors?

Part 1. Answer in 2-3 sentences per question. 1. Is your neighbourhood easy to walk around? 2. What public spaces do people in your area use most? 3. Have you ever joined a community event or workshop? 4. Would you like more green spaces where you live?

speakingPrompts.task: Part 2 · Cue card: A walking route you know
speakingPrompts.focus: Extended description with detail and limitation
speakingPrompts.prompt: Part 2. Talk for 1-2 minutes. Describe a walking route in a city or town that you know. You should say: • where the route is and what places it connects • what the path, scenery, and facilities are like • who uses this route and when • and explain what improvement you would suggest and why. You have about one minute to prepare.

Part 3. Discuss in more depth. 1. Why might some public-health messages be remembered but not followed? 2. How can organisers check whether a campaign has actually changed behaviour, not just awareness? 3. What are the limitations of using social media as the main source of health information?

speakingPrompts.task: Part 3 · Funding learning and improving public spaces
speakingPrompts.prompt: Part 3. Discuss in more depth. 1. Should students pay extra for field courses that involve travel, or should universities find other funding? Why? 2. When a city has limited money, how should leaders decide between improving a walking route and repairing transport? 3. How can small changes to public paths affect how often people walk?
